cover.headline: Small-town India's value department store, still compounding at ~18% with double-digit same-store growth; the PE overhang and the retail de-rating have halved the multiple: BUY
cover.lead: Vishal Mega Mart runs 819 leased stores (13.8 mn sq ft, 559 cities, ~74% in Tier 2 and smaller towns) selling apparel, general merchandise and FMCG, three-quarters under its own brands. Q1FY27: revenue +18.7%, same-store sales growth (SSSG) 10% (DMart 5.5%), profit +26%. Management plans ~100 large stores a year plus small-format stores. We forecast EPS of ₹2.18 / ₹2.74 / ₹3.38 for FY27-29E, a little below the street. The street values VMM on **one-year-forward P/E** (44-55x). VMM listed in Dec-2024, so the house rule uses its own forward P/E median over the last 12 months (45.2x) cut by the 13.0% fall in retail peers' P/E over the same window: **39.5x Sep-28E EPS of ₹3.06 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY**. Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹118; DCF only ₹84. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: Adjusted SSSG of 12.3% in FY25, 11.0% in FY26 and 10% in Q1FY27, driven by volume: 7-8% more customers and ~3% more spend each. Own brands (75.2% of Q1 revenue) price 30-50% below national FMCG leaders and carry 100% of apparel, so VMM gains share when budgets are squeezed.

~100 large-format stores a year (line of sight on ~400 over four years, ~2,000 in time) plus small formats in saturated UP and Haryana. We model 105 / 110 / 115 net additions (1125 stores, 17.9 mn sq ft by FY29E). Stores are leased: cash capex is ~₹3 cr per store and payback ~19 months (IPO-era RedSeer data).

The sponsors (Kedaara Capital, Partners Group) sold ~33% in two blocks eight months apart and still own 40.1%; the forward P/E fell from ~69x to ~37x in 12 months with no earnings miss. Apparel competition (Zudio, V2 Retail, V-Mart) is intense, inflation squeezes VMM's mass-market shoppers, and rent and minimum wages rise every year.

arguments.h: Valuation: the de-rating has gone far enough
arguments.p: At ₹101 VMM trades at 36.9x our FY28E and 33.0x Sep-28E EPS, below even the de-rated 39.5x. Our {{dcf.tp|inr}} is below every post-Q1 broker target (₹140-170, median ₹154.5). The DCF (₹84 at an 11.9% cost of capital) says the price already assumes 15+ years of growth, so this is a BUY on the multiple rule, not a deep-value call.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): Durga Puja falls in Q3FY27 (Q2 last year), so Q2 SSSG will look soft and Q3 strong; watch H1 together.
Store openings: ~833 stores at the Sep-2026 analyst meet (+38 since March); the ~100-a-year large-format pace plus 4-5 small stores a quarter.
The sponsors' remaining 40.1%: a further block would add supply (two blocks so far, Jun-2025 and Feb-2026); a clean exit would remove the overhang.
Inflation: fabric and petroleum-linked input costs (West Asia); VMM keeps entry prices fixed and passes increases only at higher price points.
New format pilot (younger, more affluent shoppers; first store in Delhi), the four-hub DC network and RFID roll-out (NCR first).

sections.title: A one-stop value store for small-town families: 74% own brands, all stores leased, ~17,000 sq ft each

blocks.p: Vishal Mega Mart sells a family's everyday needs under one roof at low prices: apparel (44.2% of FY26 revenue: men's, women's and children's clothing, footwear), general merchandise (28.5%: kitchenware, home furnishings, household essentials, toys, travel goods, small appliances) and FMCG (27%: staples, packaged food, home and personal care). Its customers are middle- and lower-middle-income households; FMCG brings them in often, apparel and GM earn the margin. 74.1% of FY26 revenue came from 26 own brands (two above ₹1,000 cr of sales, six above ₹500 cr): 100% of apparel, ~73-74% of GM and ~60% of FMCG volume. Own brands let VMM undercut national brands (FMCG 30-50% cheaper than market leaders, CEO) while earning more per item (~10pp more margin in FMCG, 3-4pp in GM: analyst meet, Sep-2026).

At Mar-26 it had 795 stores in 535 cities (819 at Jun-26) and 13.45 mn sq ft of retail space; ~74% of stores are in Tier 2 and smaller towns, the north and east are home ground (~63% of stores) and the south is the fastest-growing region (47 of FY26's 105 openings). Every store is leased on long contracts with ~15% rent escalation every three years (CFO). Goods move from one central DC and 17 third-party regional warehouses; a four-hub network is being built. A loyalty programme with 175 mn members accounts for ~95% of revenue, and VMM's own app delivers from 767 stores (~5% of revenue, cash break-even). Large-format stores (LFS, 17-18k sq ft) plus a small format (~8k sq ft) piloted in UP and Haryana: 16 small stores at Jun-2026, same revenue per sq ft and ROCE as LFS (management). A new format for younger, slightly more affluent shoppers is in pilot (first store in Delhi).

sections.title: From a bankrupt founder business to a PE-built listed chain: two owners, one IPO for sale, two big block deals

blocks.p: The Vishal name belongs to a chain that grew on debt in the 2000s and ran into distress by 2010. In 2011 TPG Capital and the Shriram Group bought its core business; the old listed company carried on as V2 Retail, now a competitor. In 2018 Kedaara Capital and Partners Group bought VMM for ~₹5,000 cr through Samayat Services LLP, which is why ₹4,284 cr of goodwill sits on the balance sheet. Under CEO Gunender Kapur (ex-HUL) the business pushed own brands, added FMCG and roughly doubled its store count. The Dec-2024 IPO was a pure offer for sale: the company received no money, and the sponsor has since sold down in two large blocks.

blocks.callout: **Impact on the numbers:** none of these events changed the operating accounts (no acquisitions or demergers since 2020), but they matter for the stock: the share count rises only through ESOPs (450.9 cr shares in Apr-2024, 468.4 cr in Jun-2026; 5.6 cr options still outstanding), the goodwill halves reported ROE, and the sponsor's remaining 40.1% is the main supply risk.

sections.title: Indian retail: ~₹70 trn and still ~80% unorganised; value retail in small towns is the fastest-growing corner, and the most crowded

blocks.p: Indian retail ~Rs68-72 trn in CY2023, projected Rs104-112 trn by CY2028 (~9% a year); organised retail Rs14.9 trn (CY2023) to Rs36-38 trn by CY2028 (~20% a year); unorganised still ~80% (AR FY26 MD&A, industry report; HSIE initiation 13-Apr-2026).

bullets: **Value retail is booming, and crowding.** Listed value retailers grew revenue ~25% y/y in Q1FY27 on ~20% area growth and ~5% sales per sq ft growth (MOSL sector note, 25-Sep-2026): V2 Retail +58% (73% area growth, 56 new stores in the quarter), V-Mart and Baazar Style Retail growing high-teens to 20s. VMM's 10% SSSG compares with 5.5% at DMart and ~7% at Reliance's big-box grocery (Emkay, 23-Jul-2026).

**DMart is a neighbour, not the main rival.** VMM is strongest in the north and east (~63% of 793 stores at FY26); DMart in the west and south (~84% of its 500). Over half of DMart's stores are in towns of 1 mn+; VMM's core is the 50-250k population band (~39% of stores). In the west ~45% of VMM's 75 stores and in the south ~44% of its 217 stores are in towns with no DMart (HSIE initiation, 13-Apr-2026).

**Quick commerce matters less in VMM's towns.** QC is a smaller threat in VMM's towns than in metros: VMM's own hyperlocal service reaches 767 stores; QC drives 6-8% of store revenue where organised competition is thin, 2-3% in crowded urban centres (HSIE). VMM's customers put absolute price ahead of convenience, and QC players lack VMM's own-brand SKUs.
**Whitespace.** HSIE maps ~1,246 more large-format stores (to ~2,039), 59% in the south and west; management (Sep-2026) speaks of ~1,200 more LFS plus ~4,000 small-format stores.

**Apparel is the contested category.** Trent's Zudio, V2 Retail, V-Mart and Baazar Style Retail all target the same young, value-seeking shopper in Tier 2-3 towns; management says no new competitor or step-up in expansion pace appeared in Q1FY27 (CEO, 23-Jul-2026).

blocks.callout: **What matters for VMM:** the shift from unorganised to organised retail in small towns has years to run, and VMM's mix (FMCG traffic plus own-brand apparel and GM) is hard to copy. But apparel, its biggest and most profitable category, is where the new value chains are expanding fastest.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** the tailwinds reach VMM, and its numbers show it: SSSG has stayed at 10-13% while DMart's fell to 5.5%, and revenue per sq ft rose from ₹7,853 (FY23) to ₹10,079 (FY26). The risk is not the tailwind but how many others share it in the same towns.

sections.title: The store engine: area +10-11% a year and revenue per sq ft +9-10%, the two halves of ~20% growth

blocks.p: VMM opened 105 stores in FY26 (6 closures, 99 net) and 27 in Q1FY27 (3 closures), reaching 819 stores and 13.8 mn sq ft at Jun-26 and ~833 by the Sep-2026 analyst meet. Growth comes in two ways. First, new towns: 77 new cities in FY26, with the south (Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka) taking 47 openings and Gujarat and Maharashtra performing in line with the network (CEO, May-2026). Second, density: in UP and Haryana, where VMM has tapped ~85% of its target shoppers, it now opens ~8,000 sq ft small stores that earn the same revenue per sq ft and ROCE as large ones (16 at Jun-26). Management guides ~100 large stores a year and sees ~1,200 more large-store sites (~2,000 in all) plus ~4,000 small ones.

Productivity is the other half. Revenue per average sq ft rose from ₹7,853 in FY23 to ₹10,079 in FY26 (+7.1% / +10% / +9%), on SSSG of 13.6% / 12.3% / 11.0%. Legacy stores (5+ years old) grow at double digits too (CEO), so the network is not living off new openings. The average store is shrinking (18.3k sq ft in FY23, 16.9k at Mar-26) as small formats are added and over-sized Karnataka stores were cut back, which lifted their sales per sq ft. Refurbished stores gain 10-15% in sales (Jefferies, Sep-2026).

sections.title: Three categories, one formula: FMCG brings shoppers in, own-brand apparel and GM earn the margin

blocks.p: Apparel is the anchor: ₹5,710 cr in FY26 (44.4%), all own brands, with fashion price points growing fastest (14.7% SSSG in Q4FY26, 13.9% in Q1FY27 vs 11.1% for entry price points). General merchandise (₹3,680 cr) is household essentials (~35%), furnishings (~25%) and a long tail of toys, footwear, appliances and travel goods; Tandem kitchen appliances hold about half of that category. FMCG (₹3,480 cr) grew fastest over FY22-26 (25% a year vs 23% for the group): own brands are ~60% of FMCG volume but only ~35% of value, because they are priced far below national brands. VMM does not make own brands in indulgence categories (chocolates, soft drinks); its FMCG is made by large contract manufacturers.

pair.title: Category growth in Q1FY27: all three +18-19%
Own brands: 70.2% of revenue in FY22, 75.2% in Q1FY27

blocks.callout: **So what:** the mix gives VMM something pure apparel chains lack (weekly footfall from FMCG) and something grocers lack (a 28-29% gross margin and apparel's higher margins). Seasonality follows apparel: Q2 is weak (monsoon, pre-festive), Q3 strong (festivals, winter wear). The digital channel is 70% grocery and dilutes gross margin, but 20% of its customers are new to VMM.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** VMM has a narrow but genuine moat: it runs value stores in small towns more cheaply than anyone listed, and its own brands make the price gap visible. The evidence is SSSG of 10% or more in eight of the last nine quarters (9.6% in the ninth, festival-adjusted) while competitors expanded. It does not have pricing power, and the moat is operational (execution, sourcing, data), so it must be re-earned every season; a determined rival with deep pockets (Reliance, Trent) could erode it town by town.

sections.title: Revenue 2.9x in five years, margin up ~1pp, profit 7x: operating leverage on a lean, leased store base

blocks.p: Consolidated revenue was ₹4,452 cr in Covid-hit FY21 and ₹12,906 cr in FY26 (23.7% a year; 23.3% over FY22-26). Roughly half came from more selling space (9.1 mn sq ft at Mar-22, 13.45 mn at Mar-26) and half from same-store growth of 11-13% a year outside the FY23 post-Covid rebound (25%). Reported EBITDA margin moved from 14.8% in FY22 to 14.9% in FY26; on the company's own pre-Ind AS 116, pre-ESOP basis (rent treated as a cost) the margin rose from 8.4% in FY24 to 10.2% in FY26. Because depreciation (mostly leased-store amortisation) and lease interest grew slower than sales, net profit rose from ₹203 cr to ₹839 cr (43% a year). No exceptional items in any year.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** this is a growth-plus-leverage story, not a margin-expansion one. Management reinvests gross-margin gains in price, so the margin rises only because rent (escalating ~5% a year) and head office grow slower than same-store sales. That holds while SSSG stays near 10%; at 5% it would stall.

bullets: **Growth:** SSSG 10% from 7-8% more customers and ~3% more spend per existing customer; fashion price points +13.9%. All three categories grew 18-19%. The CEO expects the inflation drag on demand to "taper down" in later quarters.

**Margins:** gross margin +30bp (fewer promotions, no significant price increases); employee cost +25% on minimum-wage rises in Haryana, UP, Telangana and Karnataka ("a structural change", CFO); ESOP cost fell to ₹8 cr (₹12.6 cr). Operating margin 10.4% (10.3%).

**Guidance (analyst meet, Sep-2026):** Analyst meet (Sep-2026): ~100 large-format stores a year with line of sight on ~400 over four years and room for ~1,200 more LFS (~2,000 in all); small formats incremental (runway ~4,000; 4-5 a quarter per Morgan Stanley). Q1 call: '80 to 100 store guidance' (analyst's words, not disputed). 833 stores at the Sep-2026 meet.

**Growth and margins:** Double-digit SSSG is the 'north star' (annual, not every quarter), volume-led; 18-20% revenue growth over the next 2-3 years (HSIE, 25-Sep-2026). Festive season falls in Q3FY27 vs Q2 last year. Gross-margin gains reinvested in product quality and price; ~50% of raw-material inflation absorbed by vendors; no price increases on opening price points; rent escalation ~15% every 3 years (~5% a year), so double-digit SSSG gives operating leverage (CFO, May-2026).
**Inflation:** West Asia crisis: fabric prices +10-11% (May-2026); selective increases at higher price points only (Jul-2026).

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** Q1 showed the model working under stress: double-digit SSSG and a stable margin while inputs and wages inflated. The festival shift (Durga Puja in Q3FY27 vs Q2 last year) will make Q2 look weak and Q3 strong; judge H1 and H2 together.

sections.title: Asset-light: cash capex ~2.5% of revenue, ₹674 cr of cash left after rent in FY26; ROE 12.1% reported, ~32% excluding goodwill

blocks.p: Every store is leased, so the cash cost of growth is fit-out, DCs and IT: ₹325 cr in FY26 (₹264 cr in FY25), ~₹3 cr per new store. The real "capex" is the lease: ₹718 cr of new right-of-use assets were signed in FY26 and rent payments (lease principal ₹453 cr + interest ₹170 cr) were ₹623 cr. Even after rent, operating cash of ₹1,621 cr left ₹674 cr, which (with ₹124 cr of ESOP proceeds) doubled cash and liquid funds to ₹1,714 cr. No dividend has been paid. Reported ROE (12.1%) is held down by ₹4,284 cr of goodwill from the 2018 buyout; on tangible equity it is ~32%.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** VMM needs little capital, but its rent bill is a fixed claim that grows with every store: ₹613 cr in FY26 (4.7% of revenue). We treat new leases as capex in the forecasts and the DCF, so the valuation pays for them. With no debt, rising cash and no dividend policy, a payout is a matter for the board (CEO, May-2026).

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean accounts, no one-offs; watch the lease accounting, the ESOP charge and the promoter's logistics contracts

bullets: **Rent is below EBITDA.** Under Ind AS 116 the ₹613 cr FY26 rent bill becomes depreciation and interest, so reported EBITDA (14.6% company basis) is far above the company's own operating EBITDA (10.2%). PBT is the fair yardstick; we treat new leases as capex.
**Cash conversion is good after rent.** CFO ₹1,621 cr less rent paid (₹623 cr) = ₹999 cr, 76% of operating EBITDA after tax; customers pay at the till and suppliers fund most inventory.

**No one-offs.** No exceptional items in FY22-26 or Q1FY27. Other income (₹86.3 cr in FY26) is mostly gains on liquid funds (₹64.8 cr) and deposit interest, and rises as cash builds: we forecast ₹{{F.otherIncome.0|num}} / {{F.otherIncome.1|num}} / {{F.otherIncome.2|num}} cr.

**ESOPs are a real cost.** ₹50 cr in FY26 (₹59 cr in FY25), ~4.5% of PBT, charged in employee cost; 5.6 cr options (1.2% of shares, average exercise price ₹45) were outstanding at Mar-26. The company's "adjusted PAT" adds the charge back; we do not.

**Related parties.** The promoter, Samayat Services LLP, billed ₹72 cr of transport and ₹31 cr of warehousing in FY26 (₹87 cr in FY25): ~0.8% of revenue paid to the controlling shareholder for logistics.

**Classification.** Screener puts bank and card charges (₹32 cr) in finance cost, so its FY26 EBITDA (₹1,918 cr) is ₹34 cr above the company's (₹1,884 cr); the model uses Screener's basis consistently.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Unmodified audit by Walker Chandiok (Grant Thornton network), one reporting segment, quarterly presentations with SSSG, area and category data. The ₹4,284 cr goodwill is the main balance-sheet judgement; an impairment would hit book value, not cash.

sections.title: No bank debt: ₹1,714 cr of cash and liquid funds against ₹1,988 cr of lease liabilities; ₹4,284 cr of goodwill is 58% of equity

blocks.p: At Mar-26 VMM had no borrowings. Screener shows ₹1,988 cr of "borrowings": these are lease liabilities (₹1,988 cr, up from ₹1,729 cr). Cash, bank deposits and liquid mutual funds were ₹1,714 cr, so net debt including leases was only ₹274 cr. The largest asset is goodwill (₹4,284 cr) from the 2018 Kedaara/Partners Group buyout; it is not amortised but tested each year. Inventory is ₹2,017 cr (~80 days on Screener's basis, down from 110 in FY21; ₹1,900 cr at Jun-26), largely funded by suppliers (payables ₹1,619 cr): net trade working capital is ~15 days. Contingent liabilities are ₹127 cr, mostly vendor, customer and other claims.

sections.title: The street after Q1: eight Buy/Overweight calls, targets ₹140-170, median ₹154.5

blocks.p: Every named broker with a post-Q1 note is positive. Emkay (₹170, 55x Jun-28E EPS) and MOSL (₹165, DCF = ~34x Sep-28E pre-Ind AS EV/EBITDA, ~51x P/E) are the most bullish and kept their calls after the Sep-2026 analyst meet; Jefferies (₹160), Elara (₹159), ICICI Securities and Aditya Birla Money (₹150 each) sit in the middle; Morgan Stanley (Overweight, ₹146) and HSIE (₹140, DCF = ~44x Sep-28E EPS) are the most cautious. The median of the eight, ₹154.5, is +53% above the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹101. Targets were cut through 2026 (MOSL ₹180 in Nov-2025, Emkay ₹180 in Dec-2025) as the stock fell. Where the method is visible, brokers translate their targets into one-year-forward P/E: Emkay 55x Jun-28E EPS; HSIE DCF = ~44x Sep-28E EPS; MOSL DCF = ~34x Sep-28E pre-Ind AS EV/EBITDA, ~51x Sep-28E EPS. P/E on Sep-28E EPS is therefore our primary method; EV/EBITDA and DCF are cross-checks.

exhibit.title: Critiques we take seriously
head: Argument
rows: Bulls (Emkay, MOSL, Jefferies): double-digit SSSG with volume-led growth, a 2,000+ store runway and the lowest cost base in value retail justify 50x+ P/E on Sep/Jun-28E.
Cautious (HSIE): models only ~8% SSSG; the ~40% PE stake (two blocks in nine months) is a medium-term supply overhang; CEO is 65 and succession matters.

Our critique: the stock de-rated from the high 60s to the high 30s on one-year-forward EPS over the last 12 months without an earnings miss; the overhang and the market's retail de-rating, not the business, set the multiple.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a well-run growth retailer at a de-rated price, with a seller on the register; BUY

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's largest listed value retailer for small towns, growing revenue ~17-20% a year from ~10% more space and ~9-10% more sales per sq ft, with three-quarters of sales under its own brands, no debt, leased stores and cash piling up. The weaknesses: no pricing power by design, intense apparel competition in the same towns, rent and wage inflation, mass-market shoppers who feel inflation first, and a private-equity owner still holding 40%.

**What you are paying:** 46.3x our FY27E and 36.9x FY28E EPS. The forward P/E has fallen from ~69x a year ago to ~37x; its 12-month median is 45.2x, and listed retailers' P/E fell 13.0% against their own medians over the same window, which gives 39.5x Sep-28E EPS and {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): BUY on our rule. EV/EBITDA (₹118) agrees; a DCF at an 11.9% cost of capital (₹84) is below the price.

bullets: **Rating: BUY, target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).** Our ratings follow the upside to our 12−month target: BUY at +15% or more, HOLD between −5% and +15%, SELL below −5%.

**The rule would turn HOLD above ~₹104** and SELL above ~₹126 on today's numbers. We would raise the target if SSSG holds at 10%+ through the festival quarters and the sponsor overhang clears; we would cut it if SSSG falls towards 5% or margins slip on wages and inflation.

**This is mainly a multiple call.** Our Sep-28E EPS (₹3.06) is ~5% below the street; our 39.5x is below every broker's implied 44-55x, which is why our {{dcf.tp|inr}} is under the post-Q1 median of ₹154.5.
**Biggest swing factor:** the multiple. Each 5x of P/E is ~₹15 a share; each 1pp of SSSG is ~₹0.04 of FY28E EPS.
